name: Chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa)
short: Juice vs placebo trial in 40 healthy women: half of those given aronia juice reported complaints (not described). Meta-analysis: fasting glucose rose in a subgroup aged 50 or under. Few safety data.
text: Few safety data on chokeberry were found. In a 6-week randomised placebo-controlled trial in which 40 healthy women drank either aronia juice or a placebo drink, only half of those given aronia juice tolerated it well and the other half reported complaints, while the placebo drink was tolerated with one exception; the abstracts do not give the size of each group or say what the complaints were. A secondary analysis of the same trial reported increased LDL and VLDL lipoprotein subclasses in plasma after the intervention, which reverted after the washout period; the abstract does not say in which group or groups this was seen or whether it differed from placebo, and its conclusion discusses adaptive processes affecting lipoprotein profiles in the women who tolerated the juice. A 2025 meta-analysis of 10 randomised trials in 666 adults, with unclear or high risk of bias in several studies and very low certainty of evidence, found no significant overall effects on cardiometabolic outcomes, although a subgroup analysis suggested increased fasting blood glucose in people aged 50 or under. A 2021 meta-analysis of controlled trials lasting an average of 6 to 8 weeks described aronia supplementation as safe, and its abstract does not report adverse events; a 2018 review of five fruits, including black chokeberry, concluded from safety studies and toxicity case reports that these fruits may generally be considered safe. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
